#!/usr/bin/env bash
# "Enable once, never again": the user turns global tracking on ONE time in
# their user settings file, then works in brand-new repos with real Claude
# Code and never runs another entire command in any of them.
set -u
S="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
T="$S/real5"; rm -rf "$T"; mkdir -p "$T/config" "$T/bin" "$T/srv/acme" "$T/work" "$T/elsewhere"
ln -sf "$S/entire-bin" "$T/bin/entire"
export PATH="$T/bin:$PATH" ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR="$T/config" ENTIRE_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT=1 GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=debug
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL="$T/gitconfig"
git config --file "$GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL" user.name "Test User"; git config --file "$GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL" user.email "test@example.com"
git config --file "$GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL" commit.gpgsign false; git config --file "$GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL" init.defaultBranch main
PORT=9422; git daemon --reuseaddr --base-path="$T/srv" --export-all --enable=receive-pack --port=$PORT --detach --pid-file="$T/daemon.pid"; sleep 1
trap 'kill $(cat "$T/daemon.pid") 2>/dev/null' EXIT
PASS=0; FAIL=0; ENTIRE_CMDS=()
ok(){ PASS=$((PASS+1)); echo "  ✓ $1"; }; bad(){ FAIL=$((FAIL+1)); echo "  ✗ $1"; }
check(){ if eval "$2" >/dev/null 2>&1; then ok "$1"; else bad "$1"; fi; }
say(){ echo; echo "▶ $1"; }
user_runs_entire(){ ENTIRE_CMDS+=("entire $*"); echo "    $ entire $*"; entire "$@" 2>&1 | grep -v '^Warning: global' | sed 's/^/    /'; }
claude_run(){ local out="$1" prompt="$2"; shift 2
  env -u CLAUDECODE -u CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT claude -p "$prompt" --model haiku --permission-mode acceptEdits --output-format json "$@" > "$out" 2>/dev/null < /dev/null
  echo "    claude → $(jq -r '.result|.[:70]' "$out" 2>/dev/null) (session $(jq -r '.session_id|.[:8]' "$out"))"; }
newrepo(){ git init -q --bare "$T/srv/acme/$2.git"; git init -q "$1"; ( cd "$1" && git remote add origin git://localhost:$PORT/acme/$2.git && echo "# $2" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m init && git push -q -u origin main ); }
# One repo's full user journey: run Claude, commit, push. No entire commands.
journey(){ local dir="$1" name="$2"
  cd "$dir"
  echo "    (no .entire/ here: $(test ! -e .entire && echo confirmed))"
  claude_run "$T/$name.json" "Create $name.txt containing the line '$name'. Do not run git commands."
  check "$name: session captured"           "ls .git/entire-sessions/*.json | grep -v trail-scope | grep -q ."
  check "$name: worktree clean except the new file" "test \"\$(git status --porcelain)\" = '?? $name.txt'"
  check "$name: still no .entire/ in the worktree"  "! test -e .entire"
  echo "    $ entire status  (read-only; shown for you, not needed by the user)"; entire status 2>&1 | sed -n '1,3p' | sed 's/^/      /'
  check "$name: status says Tracked globally"  "entire status 2>/dev/null | grep -q '● Tracked globally'"
  git add "$name.txt" && git commit -q -m "add $name"
  check "$name: commit carries a checkpoint"   "git log -1 --format=%B | grep -q '^Entire-Checkpoint: '"
  git push origin main 2>"$T/$name.push"; grep -E 'entire|held' "$T/$name.push" | sed 's/^/    push| /'
  check "$name: checkpoints synced on this push, no prompt, no hold" "! grep -q held $T/$name.push && git ls-remote origin | grep -q entire/checkpoints"
}

say "Clean machine: no user settings, no repos, Entire never run anywhere"
check "no user settings file yet" "! test -e $T/config/settings.json"

say "THE ONE-TIME STEP — the user edits their settings file once and runs one entire command"
cat > "$T/config/settings.json" <<'EOF'
{ "global": { "enabled": true, "trust_all": true } }
EOF
echo "    wrote ~/.config/entire/settings.json: $(tr -d '\n' < $T/config/settings.json)"
user_runs_entire status
check "user-level Claude hooks present in ~/.claude/settings.json" "grep -q 'entire hooks claude-code' $HOME/.claude/settings.json"

say "REPO 1 — brand-new project under ~/work; the user only runs Claude, commits, pushes"
newrepo "$T/work/alpha" alpha; journey "$T/work/alpha" alpha

say "REPO 2 — another new project in a completely different folder"
newrepo "$T/elsewhere/beta" beta; journey "$T/elsewhere/beta" beta

say "REPO 3 — a repo the user CLONES (a teammate's project, no Entire setup in it)"
git init -q --bare "$T/srv/acme/gamma.git"; ( d=$(mktemp -d); git init -q $d && cd $d && git remote add origin git://localhost:$PORT/acme/gamma.git && echo "# gamma" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -q -m init && git push -q -u origin main; rm -rf $d )
git clone -q git://localhost:$PORT/acme/gamma.git "$T/work/gamma"; journey "$T/work/gamma" gamma

say "Tally of entire commands the user ran across the whole session:"
printf '    %s\n' "${ENTIRE_CMDS[@]}"
check "exactly one entire command, and it was not 'enable'" "test ${#ENTIRE_CMDS[@]} -eq 1 && ! printf '%s' \"${ENTIRE_CMDS[*]}\" | grep -q enable"
echo; echo "==================== $PASS passed, $FAIL failed ===================="

Here it is, clean and end to end. Fresh sandbox, real Claude Code (haiku), three repos that had never seen Entire.

## The one-time step

```
wrote ~/.config/entire/settings.json:  { "global": { "enabled": true, "trust_all": true } }
$ entire status        ← the only entire command the user runs, ever
```
That single command installed the user-level Claude Code hooks (`✓ user-level Claude hooks present in ~/.claude/settings.json`). *(The status printout there shows `● Enabled` and my own live session because my shell happened to be sitting in an old enabled sandbox repo — irrelevant to the demo; the important line is `global tracking: on (2 agents covered)`.)*

## Then the user just works — three repos, zero Entire commands

| | alpha (`git init` under `~/work`) | beta (`git init` in an unrelated folder) | gamma (`git clone` of a teammate's repo, no Entire in it) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude turn | wrote `alpha.txt` | wrote `beta.txt` | wrote `gamma.txt` |
| session captured | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `git status` shows only the new file | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| no `.entire/` ever appears in the worktree | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `entire status` (read-only, shown for you) | `● Tracked globally` | `● Tracked globally` | `● Tracked globally` |
| `git commit` | `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer | trailer | trailer |
| `git push` | `Pushing entire/checkpoints/v1 to origin... done` — no prompt, no hold | same | same |

**Tally of `entire` commands the user ran in the whole session: 1 — `entire status`. `entire enable` was never run.** 21/21 checks.

Two notes on the "never again" framing:
- With `trust_all: true` in that one edit (what answering **Always** at the first push prompt writes), consent is also settled once, machine-wide — which is what you see above: pushes just sync.
- Without `trust_all`, the one per-repo thing a user ever does is answer the push prompt (or `entire trust`) the first time a repo pushes checkpoints — that's the consent gate, by design. Everything else — hooks, capture, layout, checkpoints — is still zero-touch per repo, as the earlier suites showed.

content.content:
########## 01M15BDEB2ZHEDY693TZRA7PWY
`PushQueuedCheckpointRefs` gates on `settings.CheckpointEgressAllowed(ctx)`, which keys consent on the *elected* sync remote (`resolveTrustSyncRemote` → `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote`, ignoring any explicit override), but the actual push target is the `remote` parameter passed by the caller (`resolvePushSettings(ctx, remote)` → `ps.remote`/`pushTarget()`). `doctor_migrate.go`'s `resolveMigratePushRemote` lets `--remote` supply an arbitrary remote name that need not match the elected one. If the elected remote is trusted but `--remote` names a different, untrusted remote, the gate passes and checkpoint refs are pushed to a destination consent was never actually evaluated for — a trust-boundary bypass via the migration command's explicit remote override.

########## 01M15BDEAY6RSV9SVB1PQZE859
In `runStatusJSON`, `result.Enabled` correctly accounts for `info.excludedHere()` (line ~1244: `s.Enabled && !info.excludedHere()`), but this block's guard is the raw `s.Enabled`, not the effective `result.Enabled`. For an excluded repo with repo-level `enabled: true`, `--json` reports `enabled:false` while still populating `Agents`, `SecretScanners`, `HooksOutdated`, `CheckpointSyncRemote`, and `ActiveSessions` — misleading output that diverges from the text path (`formatExcludedStatusShort`, which returns early and shows none of this). Worse, `collectActiveSessionsJSON(ctx)` calls `finalizeExitedSessions`, which can condense sessions and mutate session state — so a read-only `entire status --json` on an excluded repo performs writes that the equivalent text-mode `entire status` does not. The guard should key on `result.Enabled`, not `s.Enabled`.

########## 01M15AR6BD1F5Q6KG48WEJK6JG
`globalRuntimeRoot` is only populated when the repo's *current* policy classification is still `ActivationGlobal` (`policy.ActivationSource == repopolicy.ActivationGlobal`). If global tracking was later turned off machine-wide, or this repo became excluded (`exclude_paths`/`exclude_origins`), `ClassifyRepoPolicy` now returns `ActivationInactive`, so `runUninstall` silently skips detecting/reporting/removing the leftover `<git-common-dir>/entire/worktree/<key>` data — the very data the comment above says uninstall should remove "so uninstall means what it says." There is no other sweep of this directory (`clean.go`'s temp-file cleanup has the same gap), so locally captured session/checkpoint data from a repo's globally-tracked period can be left on disk indefinitely after the user believes they've fully uninstalled Entire.

########## 01M15968GQS2X0GFH0KFY5ERZG
`runtimeRootForPath` gates runtime-data routing on `filepath.Clean(policy.WorktreeRoot) != filepath.Clean(root)`, failing closed with `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath` on any mismatch. `root` comes from `paths.WorktreeRoot()`, which is the raw `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` output with no symlink resolution, while `policy.WorktreeRoot` comes from `repopolicy.ResolveRepositoryAt`, which resolves the same path through `filepath.EvalSymlinks` (`repository.go:64`). A worktree reachable through a symlinked path component (e.g. a symlinked project directory, or platform symlinks like `/tmp` → `/private/tmp`) will diverge between these two computations and spuriously trip this new fail-closed check, silently disabling `.entire/metadata`/`logs`/`tmp` (and thus checkpoint/session capture) for an otherwise valid repo.

########## 01M15968GNJSCW290D9K492TWH
In `runStatusJSON`, `result.Enabled` is correctly adjusted to `s.Enabled && !info.excludedHere()`, but the block that populates `Agents`, `SecretScanners`, `HooksOutdated`, `CheckpointSyncRemote`, and `ActiveSessions` is still guarded by the raw `s.Enabled` a few lines below. For a repo that is repo-level enabled but globally excluded, `--json` output reports `"enabled": false` while simultaneously populating fields as if the repo were active, contradicting the human-readable status path which short-circuits correctly for this case.

########## 01M15968GHKYBMKH3F03JCY49X
`heldCheckpointCount` (used by both `entire trust --remote <name>` in `trust_cmd.go` and `entire status`) calls `strategy.ResolveCheckpointSyncRemote(ctx)`, which never consults the pending override set by `strategy.WithSyncRemoteOverride` (only `trust_sync_remote.go`'s resolver does). So after `entire trust --remote fork` succeeds, the "N held checkpoint(s) will sync on your next push" line is computed against the currently-elected remote (e.g. `origin`) instead of `fork`, giving the user an inaccurate count for the remote they just trusted.

########## 01M15968GEJN1ND5D26ZQ1R6P6
`RevokeCurrentRepo` swallows `identityErr` and falls back to `TrustIdentity{Path: repository.WorktreeRoot}` with a nil `OriginKeys`. Since `slices.Contains(nil, ...)` is always false, the `TrustedOrigins` `DeleteFunc` below becomes a no-op, so any origin-keyed trust grant is left in place while `runTrustRevoke` still prints "✓ Revoked trust". This is the opposite of `TrustCurrentRepo`'s fail path (same file), which returns the error instead of silently degrading, so a user who explicitly revokes trust can be left with stale, still-active origin trust.

content.text:
Yes, exactly that. And no new config file was invented — `~/.config/entire/settings.json` already existed as Entire's per-user file (yours is dated Aug 12; `contexts.json`, `version_check.json` live next to it). The branch added a `global` section to it.

Why not put `global.enabled` in a repo's `.entire/settings.json`:

- **Scope.** That file lives *inside one repo* and is committed. "Track every repo on this machine" has to be written somewhere that exists before any repo does and applies to all of them — there's no repo file that can say anything about *other* repos, or about ones you haven't cloned yet.
- **Ownership.** `.entire/settings.json` is the team's decision and travels with `git clone`; `global.enabled` is your machine's decision and must not travel. If it lived in the repo file, cloning a repo would switch on machine-wide tracking for whoever cloned it.

So: **repo file = committed, per project, shared. User file = not committed, per machine, yours.** Global enable is a machine setting, hence the user file.

One historical note: the original stack *did* have an `entire enable --global` command and a wizard that wrote this same user file; the Aug 24 refactor (`b37e531db "make activation settings-only"`) removed the command and kept the file as the single source of truth. So today the "once" is editing that file (and any `entire` command installs the hooks). If you want the command back as a convenience wrapper over the same file, that's a small, separate change.

Continuing with the review fixes — build passed on the five edits; next I'm locating the uninstall code for the leftover-runtime-dir finding, then tests, full check, commit, push.

func TestPushQueuedCheckpointRefs_EgressGateHoldsUntrustedRepo(t *testing.T) {
	testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv(t)
	workDir, bareDir, refs := setupRepoWithCheckpointRefs(t)
	t.Chdir(workDir)
	enrollRepoGlobally(t, `{"global":{"enabled":true}}`)

	repo, err := git.PlainOpen(workDir)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	queue := enqueueRefs(t, repo, refs)

	_, pushDisabled, err := PushQueuedCheckpointRefs(context.Background(), repo, bareDir)
	require.ErrorContains(t, err, "entire trust")
	assert.False(t, pushDisabled, "a trust hold is not push_sessions=false")

	remaining, err := queue.Drain()
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.ElementsMatch(t, refs, remaining, "a held push leaves refs queued")
}

fix(global): close the second review round — push-target consent, revoke fails loud, JSON guard, uninstall leftovers, held count under --remote

Trail 1074 findings on the previous head, each verified against the code:

- PushQueuedCheckpointRefs evaluated consent for the ELECTED remote while
  pushing to the caller's remote (`doctor migrate --remote`), so a trusted
  election could release refs to an unconsented destination. When the target
  is a configured remote other than the election, the policy is re-derived
  for it (the same pending-election path pre-push uses) before the gate; a
  raw URL/path target keeps the election's consent as the only one there is.
- RevokeCurrentRepo swallowed an identity error and fell back to a path-only
  identity, so the TrustedOrigins delete was a no-op under a "✓ Revoked".
  It now returns the error, matching TrustCurrentRepo.
- runStatusJSON populated agents, sync remote and active sessions (and ran
  the exited-session sweep) for a repo it had just reported enabled:false;
  the block is guarded by the effective state now.
- disable --uninstall only looked for global-mode runtime data while the repo
  still classified as ActivationGlobal, so a tier turned off (or a later
  exclusion) left <git-common-dir>/entire/worktree/<key> behind. It is now
  located from repository identity (Repository.GlobalRuntimeRoot), which
  RuntimeRoot also uses.
- heldCheckpointCount ignored `entire trust --remote X`, reporting the count
  for the election. ResolveCheckpointSyncRemoteForTrust honors the override.
- runtimeRootForPath's worktree-identity check: the reported symlink
  mismatch does not reproduce (git canonicalizes --show-toplevel; verified

content.text:
# Comprehensive PR Review

Run a comprehensive pull request review using multiple specialized agents, each focusing on a different aspect of code quality.

**Review Aspects (optional):** "2030"

## Review Workflow:

1. **Determine Review Scope**
   - Check git status to identify changed files
   - Parse arguments to see if user requested specific review aspects
   - Default: Run all applicable reviews

2. **Available Review Aspects:**

   - **comments** - Analyze code comment accuracy and maintainability
   - **tests** - Review test coverage quality and completeness
   - **errors** - Check error handling for silent failures
   - **types** - Analyze type design and invariants (if new types added)
   - **code** - General code review for project guidelines
   - **simplify** - Simplify code for clarity and maintainability
   - **all** - Run all applicable reviews (default)

3. **Identify Changed Files**
   - Run `git diff --name-only` to see modified files
   - Check if PR already exists: `gh pr view`
   - Identify file types and what reviews apply

4. **Determine Applicable Reviews**

   Based on changes:
   - **Always applicable**: code-reviewer (general quality)
   - **If test files changed**: pr-test-analyzer
   - **If comments/docs added**: comment-analyzer
   - **If error handling changed**: silent-failure-hunter
   - **If types added/modified**: type-design-analyzer
   - **After passing review**: code-simplifier (polish and refine)

5. **Launch Review Agents**

   **Sequential approach** (one at a time):
   - Easier to understand and act on
   - Each report is complete before next
   - Good for interactive review

   **Parallel approach** (user can request):
   - Launch all agents simultaneously
   - Faster for comprehensive review
   - Results come back together

6. **Aggregate Results**

   After agents complete, summarize:
   - **Critical Issues** (must fix before merge)
   - **Important Issues** (should fix)
   - **Suggestions** (nice to have)
   - **Positive Observations** (what's good)

7. **Provide Action Plan**

   Organize findings:
   ```markdown
   # PR Review Summary

   ## Critical Issues (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Issue description [file:line]

   ## Important Issues (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Issue description [file:line]

   ## Suggestions (X found)
   - [agent-name]: Suggestion [file:line]

   ## Strengths
   - What's well-done in this PR

   ## Recommended Action
   1. Fix critical issues first
   2. Address important issues
   3. Consider suggestions
   4. Re-run review after fixes
   ```

## Usage Examples:

**Full review (default):**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr
```

**Specific aspects:**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr tests errors
# Reviews only test coverage and error handling

/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr comments
# Reviews only code comments

/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr simplify
# Simplifies code after passing review
```

**Parallel review:**
```
/pr-review-toolkit:review-pr all parallel
# Launches all agents in parallel
```

## Agent Descriptions:

**comment-analyzer**:
- Verifies comment accuracy vs code
- Identifies comment rot
- Checks documentation completeness

**pr-test-analyzer**:
- Reviews behavioral test coverage
- Identifies critical gaps
- Evaluates test quality

**silent-failure-hunter**:
- Finds silent failures
- Reviews catch blocks
- Checks error logging

**type-design-analyzer**:
- Analyzes type encapsulation
- Reviews invariant expression
- Rates type design quality

**code-reviewer**:
- Checks CLAUDE.md compliance
- Detects bugs and issues
- Reviews general code quality

**code-simplifier**:
- Simplifies complex code
- Improves clarity and readability
- Applies project standards
- Preserves functionality

## Tips:

- **Run early**: Before creating PR, not after
- **Focus on changes**: Agents analyze git diff by default
- **Address critical first**: Fix high-priority issues before lower priority
- **Re-run after fixes**: Verify issues are resolved
- **Use specific reviews**: Target specific aspects when you know the concern

## Workflow Integration:

**Before committing:**
```
1. Write code
2. Run: /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr code errors
3. Fix any critical issues
4. Commit
```

**Before creating PR:**
```
1. Stage all changes
2. Run: /pr-review-toolkit:review-pr all
3. Address all critical and important issues
4. Run specific reviews again to verify
5. Create PR
```

**After PR feedback:**
```
1. Make requested changes
2. Run targeted reviews based on feedback
3. Verify issues are resolved
4. Push updates
```

## Notes:

- Agents run autonomously and return detailed reports
- Each agent focuses on its specialty for deep analysis
- Results are actionable with specific file:line references
- Agents use appropriate models for their complexity
- All agents available in `/agents` list

<result>## Type design review — PR #2030 `feat/global-trust` (head 7ac91dd4f)

Scope read: `cmd/entire/cli/settings/repopolicy/{types,repository,sync_remote,trust,policy,activation,user_settings}.go`, `settings/{global,trust}.go`, `strategy/{trust_prompt,trust_sync_remote,checkpoint_sync_remote,manual_commit_push}.go`, `paths/invisible.go`, `internal/worktreeid/worktreeid.go`, `status.go`, `hook_policy.go`, `setup.go` (uninstall), plus `docs/architecture/global-tracking.md` and the seam-mutating tests.

Overall: the *behavioral* invariants (activation derived-not-recorded, exclusive origin-or-path identity, trust_all before identity, per-block strictness, RuntimeRoot as a function of activation source) are all implemented correctly and documented unusually well. The weakness is structural: almost every invariant lives in the constructor functions and the doc comments, and every struct is an open bag of exported fields, so the same invariants are violable by any literal. Because the package is a leaf that other packages construct into (`hook_policy.go` mutates a `RepoPolicy` in place; tests build literals), that is not purely hypothetical.

---

## Type: `RepoPolicy` (`repopolicy/types.go:92`)

### Invariants identified
- `Active == (ActivationSource != ActivationInactive)`; `InactiveReason == None` iff `Active`. Three fields encode one three-valued state.
- `WorktreeRoot`, `GitCommonDir`, `WorktreeKey` are a copy of a `Repository` and must agree with it (`WorktreeKey == runtimeKey(worktreeid)`).
- When `ActivationSource == Global`, `GitCommonDir` and `WorktreeKey` are non-empty (otherwise `RuntimeRoot()` returns `""`).
- `Trust` is meaningful only when `Active`; `ClassifyActivationAt` deliberately leaves it zero.
- Snapshot semantics: once attached via `WithRepoPolicy`, treated as immutable.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 3/10** — all fields exported; `hook_policy.go:25-30` rewrites `Active/ActivationSource/InactiveReason` by hand outside the package. Nothing prevents `Active: true, ActivationSource: ActivationInactive`.
- **Invariant expression: 6/10** — the `RuntimeRoot()` doc and the `ClassifyRepoPolicyAt` precedence comment are excellent; the redundancy of `Active` + `ActivationSource` + `InactiveReason` is not expressed anywhere.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — a single classification snapshot on `ctx` is exactly the right shape for a hook process; `RuntimeRoot()` being a pure function of the source is the load-bearing design and it is right.
- **Invariant enforcement: 4/10** — enforced only inside `classifyActivationAt`/`ClassifyGlobalConfig`. `RuntimeRoot()` has no guard: a Global policy with empty `GitCommonDir` yields `""`, and `paths.runtimeRootForPath` (`invisible.go:79`) hands that straight back, so `filepath.Join("", "metadata", ...)` becomes a CWD-relative path — one session split across roots, the exact failure `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath` exists to prevent. Today only reachable from a literal, but there is no check standing between a future refactor and that outcome.

### Strengths
- Value type, cheap to copy, context-carried; the "never persisted" contract is stated at the type.
- `ClassifyActivationAt` vs `ClassifyRepoPolicyAt` split (no egress for foreign roots) is a real invariant captured in the API rather than a flag.

### Concerns
- **Real bug risk (low probability, high blast radius):** `RuntimeRoot()` can return `""`. Add a guard that returns an error or panics on incomplete Global identity, or make `paths.runtimeRootForPath` reject `""` with `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath`. Cost: ~5 lines.
- Mixing three concerns (activation, repo identity, trust) is defensible for a snapshot, but the identity triple should be the `Repository` value itself, not three copied strings — `DecideEgress(ctx, policy, global, repository)` already takes both, so they can disagree.
- `hook_policy.go` reaches in and flips three fields. That is the one place the invariant is maintained by an outside caller.

### Recommended improvements
1. Replace `Active bool` with a method `func (p RepoPolicy) Active() bool { return p.ActivationSource != ActivationInactive }` (or keep the field but make `InactiveReason` the only source of truth). Cost: mechanical rename across ~15 call sites; removes a whole class of literal-induced inconsistency.
2. Embed `Repository` instead of copying three fields: `RepoPolicy{ Repository; ActivationSource; InactiveReason; Trust }`. `RuntimeRoot()` becomes `p.Repository.GlobalRuntimeRoot()`; `DecideEgress` drops a parameter. Cost: small, one-time.
3. Give `hook_policy.go` a package method, e.g. `func (p RepoPolicy) Deactivated(reason InactiveReason) RepoPolicy`, so the outside caller cannot half-update the tuple. Cost: trivial.

---

## Type: `TrustIdentity` (`types.go:53`)

### Invariants identified
- Exactly one of `OriginKeys` (non-empty) or `Path` (non-empty) is set — "the flip is whole".
- `OriginKeys` are deduplicated, normalized `host/owner/repo`, lowercased.
- `RemoteName`/`Dedicated` are display-only and do not participate in matching.
- Zero value = "identity unresolved" (used under `trust_all` when resolution fails, and on `RepoTrustIdentity` error).

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 4/10** — exported slice and strings; a literal `{OriginKeys: [...], Path: "..."}` is representable and `identityTrusted` would then silently take the origin branch only.
- **Invariant expression: 6/10** — the doc comment is precise; the struct shape says "any combination".
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — the exclusivity rule and the all-URLs-must-be-listed rule are the security core of the feature and both are correct.
- **Invariant enforcement: 6/10** — `ResolveTrustIdentity` enforces exclusivity and normalization correctly; no other constructor, but nothing stops literals. `DisplayScope()` on the zero value returns `""`, which status/prompt then render as an empty scope.

### Strengths
- `OriginKeyed()` + `DisplayScope()` are the right minimal accessors; callers (`trust_prompt.go:92-97`, `setup.go:1518`, `trust_cmd.go:94`) only use these plus `RemoteName`.
- Path fallback on *any* unparseable URL (rather than partial key set) is the correct fail-closed choice and is tested.

### Concerns
- **Display fields beside the matching key**: `RemoteName`/`Dedicated` are harmless functionally, but they make the type's equality meaningless and blur "what is the consent key". This is a style/clarity issue, not a bug. A cleaner split is `TrustKey` (origins | path) and `TrustIdentity{ Key TrustKey; Remote SyncRemote }`, or just keep `SyncRemote` on `TrustDecision` instead.
- The JSON tags (`origin_keys`, `path`, `remote`, `dedicated`) have no user in the tree — dead surface that implies a serialization contract nobody honors.
- Zero value doubling as "unresolved" means `status --json` can emit `sync_remote: ""` and the prompt can fall back to "this folder only" wording when in fact resolution failed. It is not wrong, but an explicit `Resolved bool`/`error` would make the three states (origin/path/unknown) visible.

### Recommended improvements
1. Make the key a two-case sum: `type TrustKey struct{ origins []string; path string }` with unexported fields and constructors `OriginKey(keys)`/`PathKey(root)`. Cost: moderate (the settings writer `TrustCurrentRepo` iterates `OriginKeys`; expose `Origins() []string`). Benefit: exclusivity becomes unrepresentable-to-violate.
2. Drop the JSON tags until something serializes it. Cost: zero.
3. Cheaper alternative if you keep the flat struct: add `func (id TrustIdentity) valid() bool` and assert it at the end of `ResolveTrustIdentity` (a test-time tripwire). Cost: 3 lines.

---

## Type: `TrustDecision` (repopolicy, `types.go:72`)

### Invariants identified
- `Allowed => Source ∈ {Local, All, Repo} && Reason == None`.
- `!Allowed => Source == None && Reason ∈ {Inactive, Untrusted, InvalidOrigin, Settings}`.
- `Identity` is set whenever it resolved, regardless of `Allowed`; empty under `Inactive`, `InvalidOrigin`, `Settings`.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 3/10** — four exported fields; `Allowed: true, Source: None` is representable.
- **Invariant expression: 5/10** — `Allowed` is redundant with `Source != None`; reason/source are two half-enums of one outcome.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — `Source` drives real UX (banner under `trust_all`, `not_applicable` while tier is off) and `Reason` drives diagnostics.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — `DecideEgress` builds every value correctly and `TrustSourceLocal` is correctly restricted to "tier off".

### Concerns
- **Name collision (style, but a real reading hazard):** `strategy.TrustDecision` (an `int` enum: `TrustHeld`/`TrustGranted`, `trust_prompt.go:18`) and `repopolicy.TrustDecision` (this struct) share a name across two packages that both appear in `manual_commit_push.go`. Rename the strategy one `TrustPromptOutcome` (or `promptResult`). Cost: trivial.
- `computeRepoTrustState` (`status.go:271`) discards `Reason`, so `status --json` cannot distinguish "untrusted" from "user settings file unreadable" (`TrustReasonSettings`) from "election failed" (`TrustReasonInvalidOrigin`). The information exists in the type and is thrown away on the way out. Usefulness gap, cheap to fix (`trust_reason` field).

### Recommended improvements
1. Collapse to `Outcome TrustSource` where `TrustSourceNone` means held, and derive `Allowed()`; keep `Reason` for the held case. Cost: small; removes an impossible state.
2. Surface `Reason` in `globalTrackingJSON`. Cost: 3 lines.

---

## Type: `RepoActivation` (`types.go:121`) and `ReadRepoActivation` (`activation.go:50`)

### Invariants identified
- `Enabled` is meaningful only when `Configured`.
- `LocalOverride => Configured`, and the effective `Enabled` came from a trusted `settings.local.json` with an explicit key.
- A local file without an `enabled` key never sets `Configured`.
- A tracked/symlinked local file is ignored wholesale (via `LocalSettingsTrusted`).

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 4/10** — three bools, any combination constructible; `Enabled: true, Configured: false` is representable and only safe because `policy.go` checks `Configured && Enabled`.
- **Invariant expression: 7/10** — the type comment explains the "set up" notion clearly; `LocalOverride` is well named for its one consumer (the exclusion bypass at `policy.go:99`).
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — `LocalOverride` encodes exactly the trust-relevant fact ("the developer's own action on this clone outranks user exclusions, cloned content does not"); that is the right distinction and it is tested.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — `ReadRepoActivation` is the sole producer and is correct, including the null-`enabled` case.

### Concerns
- Three bools are really a four-state enum: `NotConfigured | ProjectEnabled | ProjectDisabled | Local{enabled bool}`. Modeling it as `type RepoActivation int` (or a small struct with `Source ActivationFile` + `Enabled`) would make `LocalOverride && !Configured` unrepresentable. Style preference; the code is correct as is.
- `LocalOverride` is set to `!isProject` even when no project file exists, so the name "override" is slightly off — it means "came from local", not "overrode project". The doc comment says the right thing; the identifier does not.

### Recommended improvements
- Rename to `FromLocal` or `LocalDecided`. Cost: trivial. Or fold into an enum as above; cost: small, two call sites.

---

## Type: `Repository` (`repository.go:18`)

### Invariants identified
- `WorktreeRoot` and `GitCommonDir` are absolute, symlink-canonicalized.
- `WorktreeKey == runtimeKey(WorktreeID)` (16 hex chars).
- `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` returns `""` when identity incomplete.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 4/10** — `WorktreeKey` is a derived field that can be set independently of `WorktreeID`.
- **Invariant expression: 7/10** — the 64-bit key rationale (collision would merge two worktrees' runtime state) is stated where it matters.
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` being a function of identity alone (not policy) is exactly what uninstall needs and the doc says why.
- **Invariant enforcement: 6/10** — `ResolveRepositoryAt` is the only producer and correct; `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` guards emptiness. But `RuntimeDir(repository)` in `activation.go:19` is a duplicate of `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` **without** the empty guard and has zero callers in the tree — dead code that could be picked up later and reintroduce the empty-root hazard.

### Recommended improvements
1. Delete `RuntimeDir`. Cost: zero.
2. Drop `WorktreeKey` as a field; compute it in `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` from `WorktreeID` (or unexport and expose `Key()`). Cost: small; removes a derivable-field inconsistency.

---

## Types: `SyncRemote`, `SyncRemoteResolver`, and the seams `ResolveSyncRemote` / `LocalSettingsTrusted` (`sync_remote.go`, `activation.go:32`)

### Invariants identified
- `Name == ""` ⇔ no remote ⇒ `URLs` empty ⇒ path identity.
- `URLs` deduplicated; in `Dedicated` mode exactly one derived URL.
- Seams: the real implementations are installed by `settings` (init) and `strategy` (init); the defaults are weaker/different.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 3/10** — the two seams are exported mutable package globals with no mutex, no `Set…ForTesting` accessor, and no way to tell whether the real implementation is installed.
- **Invariant expression: 7/10** — both defaults document exactly why they exist and what differs; `trust_sync_remote.go` explains the cycle.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — keying consent on the elected remote rather than `origin` is the right invariant, and routing it through one resolver is the right seam.
- **Invariant enforcement: 4/10** — see concerns.

### Concerns (this is the most important design question in the PR)
- **Link-dependent semantics.** `settings` imports `repopolicy` but does not link `strategy`. Every test in `settings` (e.g. `TestTrustCurrentRepoAndRevoke`) therefore runs against the *origin* default, not the election. Any future binary or test package that uses `settings.CheckpointEgressAllowed` without linking `strategy` silently gets pre-election semantics — a consent keyed on `origin` while checkpoints go elsewhere. Today the CLI binary links `strategy`, so production is correct, but the correctness is a property of the link graph, not of the type. Same for `LocalSettingsTrusted`: the repopolicy default (symlink-only) is strictly weaker than the installed one (index + HEAD + symlink), so a repopolicy-only test can pass a case production rejects, or vice versa.
- **Silent unguarded globals.** Tests in both packages reassign the vars and restore in `t.Cleanup`. Correct today only because those specific tests do *not* call `t.Parallel()` while `TestEgressDecision_LocalActivationIsGatedWhileGlobalIsOn` and `TestReadRepoActivation` (which read the seams) do — Go's sequential-then-parallel ordering happens to serialize them. CLAUDE.md says "always use `t.Parallel()`"; the first person who obeys that on one of the seam-mutating tests introduces a `-race` failure. Contrast `paths/invisible.go`, which wraps its test seam in an `RWMutex` — the package is inconsistent with itself.
- `Dedicated` on `SyncRemote` and again on `TrustIdentity` is the same fact copied twice.

### Recommended improvements (ordered by value/cost)
1. **Make "real resolver not installed" loud.** Keep the var but have the default *fail* (`errors.New("repopolicy.ResolveSyncRemote not installed")`) in non-test builds, or record `installed bool` and have `ResolveTrustIdentity` return an error when it is false and `!testing.Testing()`. Cost: ~10 lines. Benefit: converts a silent semantic downgrade into a hard error — this is the one change I would call a real bug-risk reduction.
2. **Replace the bare vars with `Set…ForTesting(fn) (restore func())` accessors guarded by a mutex**, mirroring `paths.SetInvisibleProbeFailureForTesting`. Cost: ~20 lines plus two test call sites. Removes the latent `t.Parallel` race.
3. Longer term: pass a `Resolver` interface through `ClassifyRepoPolicyAt` (a `PolicyDeps{SyncRemote, LocalTrusted}` param with a `Default()` in `settings`). Cost: touches every `ClassifyRepoPolicy` caller (~10). Worth it only if a third seam appears; the accessor approach is the pragmatic stop.

---

## Type: `GlobalConfig` (`types.go:135`)

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 5/10** — plain data, but that is correct for a user-edited file schema. Lists are exported slices mutated in place by `TrustCurrentRepo`/`RevokeCurrentRepo` under `ModifyUserSettings`' lock, which is the right place.
- **Invariant expression: 9/10** — the field docs are the best in the PR: every list states glob-vs-exact, cascade-vs-no-cascade, fail-closed behavior, and why trust fields live in the strict block.
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — the strict-block rationale ("a pre-trust binary must fail closed rather than misread consent") is a genuine safety invariant.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — validation is split correctly: `validateGlobalExclusions` fails closed on activation, `ValidateGlobalPatterns` adds trusted_paths for doctor only. `TrustedOrigins` entries are canonicalized on read (`CanonicalTrustOrigin`) but written raw; fine.

### Concerns
- `TrustAll bool \`json:"trust_all,omitempty"\`` — `omitempty` on a bool means a user who sets `trust_all: false` explicitly will see the key vanish on the next `entire trust` write. Cosmetic, but the file is documented as user-edited, so it is a small surprise.

---

## Type: `UserSettings` (`types.go:209`, `user_settings.go`)

### Invariants identified
- `Global == nil` ⇔ unconfigured tier.
- `global` block strict; other top-level blocks preserved byte-for-byte in `extra`.
- Whole file is one JSON value (trailing-data check).

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 8/10** — `extra` is unexported; the only mutation path is `ModifyUserSettings` (locked, atomic write). Good.
- **Invariant expression: 9/10** — type and method docs state the per-block rule and its reason.
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — forward-compat for mixed-version machines without weakening consent decoding is exactly the right trade.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — see the receiver issue.

### Concerns
- **Real bug risk (latent):** `MarshalJSON` has a pointer receiver. If any caller ever marshals a `UserSettings` *value* (embeds it by value in another struct, or `json.Marshal(*us)`), `encoding/json` will not find the method, will emit only `global` and **silently drop every preserved block**. Nothing today does that (`persistUserSettings` passes `*UserSettings`), but the failure is silent and destructive to another binary's settings. Make `MarshalJSON` a value receiver (it only reads). Cost: one token.
- `extra` is a map, so copying a `UserSettings` aliases it; harmless because the type is only produced by `LoadUserSettings` and consumed under the lock.
- `"global": null` is skipped on read and not preserved in `extra`, so a round-trip drops the key. Negligible.

---

## Types: `ActivationSource`, `TrustSource`, `TrustReason` (string) vs `InactiveReason` (int)

- **Consistency (style, but it leaks into the API):** three of the four enums are strings with stable wire values and are emitted directly (`string(info.ActivationSource)`); `InactiveReason` is an `int` and needs a hand-written `inactiveReasonJSON` mapper in `status.go:1139` plus `globalInactiveHereText`. Pick one. Strings with stable values are the better fit here since they *are* already a public JSON contract; make `InactiveReason` a string enum with the JSON values it already maps to (`repo_excluded`, `repo_disabled`, `global_off`) and delete the mapper. Cost: small; the `settings` package re-exports the constants so callers do not change.
- **Zero values:** `ActivationSource("")` is not a member (the zero is not `ActivationInactive`), so a zero `RepoPolicy` has an out-of-domain source. `TrustReasonNone == ""` and `InactiveReasonNone == 0` are the zero — inconsistent. Prefer making the zero value the "none/inactive" member for every enum so a zero struct is at least well-formed.
- `InactiveReasonGlobalOff` is overloaded: it is also what `classifyActivationAt` returns when `git rev-parse` fails and what `ClassifyGlobalConfig` returns on a nil resolver. `status.go` sidesteps this via `PolicyError`, but the type itself cannot say "unknown". A `InactiveReasonUnknown`/`ClassificationFailed` member would let the reason stand alone. Cost: one constant + two returns.
- `TrustSourceLocal = "local_activation"` is really "global tier off" (the only way an active repo can hit it). The name reads as "activated locally", which is also true of a repo-enabled repo *with* the tier on — where the source is `repo` or `trust_all`. `TrustSourceTierOff` would be truthful. Style.

---

## Types: `globalTrackingInfo`, `globalTrackingJSON`, `statusJSON` (`status.go`)

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 5/10** — unexported struct with exported fields, one producer (`computeGlobalTrackingInfo`); acceptable for an intra-package view model.
- **Invariant expression: 5/10** — five fields carry "meaningless unless X" caveats (`AgentsCovered` unless Enabled; `ActiveHere`/`InactiveReason` unless `InRepo && PolicyError == ""`; `TrustState` "" doubles as the in-repo marker). That is a lot of implicit structure for a flat struct.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — the "one computation, two renderers" rule is the right invariant and `trackedHere()`/`excludedHere()` capture the two states that matter.
- **Invariant enforcement: 6/10** — the renderers respect the caveats today; nothing stops a new renderer from reading `ActiveHere` when `PolicyError != ""`.

### Concerns
- The comment at `status.go:1183` — "TrustState doubles as the in-repo marker" — is a smell: `InRepo` already exists. Use it.
- `PolicyError` and `ActiveHere` are mutually exclusive by convention only. A small nested `*repoView{ Active, InactiveReason, TrustState, TrustSource, SyncRemote, Held }` set only on successful classification would make the "outside a repo" and "classification failed" shapes structurally different from "classified". Cost: moderate refactor of one file; only worth it if more fields are coming (they probably are).
- As noted under `TrustDecision`: `trust_reason` is dropped from JSON.

---

## Types: `strategy.TrustDecision` / `trustChoice` (`trust_prompt.go`)

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 8, Expression 8, Usefulness 8, Enforcement 8.** Small, unexported choice enum; the outcome enum is two-valued and the comment on `TrustGranted` ("the caller re-evaluates the gate, never reuses this as a boolean") is exactly the right invariant, and `manual_commit_push.go:84-111` honors it by reclassifying. `askTrustPrompt` starting with `trustChoice("")` and whitelisting the three values before returning is good accessible-mode hygiene.
- Only concern is the cross-package name clash already noted. Rename to `trustPromptOutcome`/`TrustPromptOutcome`.

---

## Type: `CheckpointSyncRemote` / `CheckpointSyncRemoteSource` (`checkpoint_sync_remote.go`)

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 5, Expression 8, Usefulness 8, Enforcement 6.** The precedence doc is thorough and the source enum matches `status --json`.
- **Real (minor) bug risk:** `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemoteForTrust` (`trust_sync_remote.go:60`) fabricates `Source: SyncRemoteSourceConfig` for an `--remote` override. The type now lies about provenance; if any renderer or `hintGatedCheckpointSync`-style check (`Source == SyncRemoteSourceConfig` suppresses the hint) ever consumes this value, it will treat a one-off override as a persistent setting. Add `SyncRemoteSourceOverride` (or return only the name). Cost: one constant.

---

## `paths/invisible.go` — `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath`, test seam

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 8, Expression 8, Usefulness 9, Enforcement 7.** Sentinel + `Is` helper, fail-closed on mismatch, and the worktree-identity check before trusting a ctx snapshot is a good defensive invariant. The mutex-guarded test seam is the pattern `repopolicy` should copy.
- Gap: does not reject `policy.RuntimeRoot() == ""` (see `RepoPolicy`). One `if root == "" { return "", ErrUnroutableRuntimePath }` closes it at the choke point regardless of what `repopolicy` does.

---

## `internal/worktreeid`

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 8, Expression 7, Usefulness 8, Enforcement 7.** Pure functions, clear main-vs-linked contract, submodule-aware parsing. Two independent hashes of the same ID exist (`worktreeid.Hash` = 6 chars for branch names, `repopolicy.runtimeKey` = 16 for directories); the reason is documented at `runtimeKey`. Fine, but consider `worktreeid.HashN(id, n)` so the two derivations share one function. Cost: trivial.

---

## Summary: real bug risks vs. style

**Real bug risks (fix in this PR or a fast follow):**
1. `UserSettings.MarshalJSON` pointer receiver — a value marshal silently drops preserved blocks. One-token fix.

<result>## Type design review — PR #2030 `feat/global-trust` (head 7ac91dd4f)

Scope read: `cmd/entire/cli/settings/repopolicy/{types,repository,sync_remote,trust,policy,activation,user_settings}.go`, `settings/{global,trust}.go`, `strategy/{trust_prompt,trust_sync_remote,checkpoint_sync_remote,manual_commit_push}.go`, `paths/invisible.go`, `internal/worktreeid/worktreeid.go`, `status.go`, `hook_policy.go`, `setup.go` (uninstall), plus `docs/architecture/global-tracking.md` and the seam-mutating tests.

Overall: the *behavioral* invariants (activation derived-not-recorded, exclusive origin-or-path identity, trust_all before identity, per-block strictness, RuntimeRoot as a function of activation source) are all implemented correctly and documented unusually well. The weakness is structural: almost every invariant lives in the constructor functions and the doc comments, and every struct is an open bag of exported fields, so the same invariants are violable by any literal. Because the package is a leaf that other packages construct into (`hook_policy.go` mutates a `RepoPolicy` in place; tests build literals), that is not purely hypothetical.

---

## Type: `RepoPolicy` (`repopolicy/types.go:92`)

### Invariants identified
- `Active == (ActivationSource != ActivationInactive)`; `InactiveReason == None` iff `Active`. Three fields encode one three-valued state.
- `WorktreeRoot`, `GitCommonDir`, `WorktreeKey` are a copy of a `Repository` and must agree with it (`WorktreeKey == runtimeKey(worktreeid)`).
- When `ActivationSource == Global`, `GitCommonDir` and `WorktreeKey` are non-empty (otherwise `RuntimeRoot()` returns `""`).
- `Trust` is meaningful only when `Active`; `ClassifyActivationAt` deliberately leaves it zero.
- Snapshot semantics: once attached via `WithRepoPolicy`, treated as immutable.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 3/10** — all fields exported; `hook_policy.go:25-30` rewrites `Active/ActivationSource/InactiveReason` by hand outside the package. Nothing prevents `Active: true, ActivationSource: ActivationInactive`.
- **Invariant expression: 6/10** — the `RuntimeRoot()` doc and the `ClassifyRepoPolicyAt` precedence comment are excellent; the redundancy of `Active` + `ActivationSource` + `InactiveReason` is not expressed anywhere.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — a single classification snapshot on `ctx` is exactly the right shape for a hook process; `RuntimeRoot()` being a pure function of the source is the load-bearing design and it is right.
- **Invariant enforcement: 4/10** — enforced only inside `classifyActivationAt`/`ClassifyGlobalConfig`. `RuntimeRoot()` has no guard: a Global policy with empty `GitCommonDir` yields `""`, and `paths.runtimeRootForPath` (`invisible.go:79`) hands that straight back, so `filepath.Join("", "metadata", ...)` becomes a CWD-relative path — one session split across roots, the exact failure `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath` exists to prevent. Today only reachable from a literal, but there is no check standing between a future refactor and that outcome.

### Strengths
- Value type, cheap to copy, context-carried; the "never persisted" contract is stated at the type.
- `ClassifyActivationAt` vs `ClassifyRepoPolicyAt` split (no egress for foreign roots) is a real invariant captured in the API rather than a flag.

### Concerns
- **Real bug risk (low probability, high blast radius):** `RuntimeRoot()` can return `""`. Add a guard that returns an error or panics on incomplete Global identity, or make `paths.runtimeRootForPath` reject `""` with `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath`. Cost: ~5 lines.
- Mixing three concerns (activation, repo identity, trust) is defensible for a snapshot, but the identity triple should be the `Repository` value itself, not three copied strings — `DecideEgress(ctx, policy, global, repository)` already takes both, so they can disagree.
- `hook_policy.go` reaches in and flips three fields. That is the one place the invariant is maintained by an outside caller.

### Recommended improvements
1. Replace `Active bool` with a method `func (p RepoPolicy) Active() bool { return p.ActivationSource != ActivationInactive }` (or keep the field but make `InactiveReason` the only source of truth). Cost: mechanical rename across ~15 call sites; removes a whole class of literal-induced inconsistency.
2. Embed `Repository` instead of copying three fields: `RepoPolicy{ Repository; ActivationSource; InactiveReason; Trust }`. `RuntimeRoot()` becomes `p.Repository.GlobalRuntimeRoot()`; `DecideEgress` drops a parameter. Cost: small, one-time.
3. Give `hook_policy.go` a package method, e.g. `func (p RepoPolicy) Deactivated(reason InactiveReason) RepoPolicy`, so the outside caller cannot half-update the tuple. Cost: trivial.

---

## Type: `TrustIdentity` (`types.go:53`)

### Invariants identified
- Exactly one of `OriginKeys` (non-empty) or `Path` (non-empty) is set — "the flip is whole".
- `OriginKeys` are deduplicated, normalized `host/owner/repo`, lowercased.
- `RemoteName`/`Dedicated` are display-only and do not participate in matching.
- Zero value = "identity unresolved" (used under `trust_all` when resolution fails, and on `RepoTrustIdentity` error).

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 4/10** — exported slice and strings; a literal `{OriginKeys: [...], Path: "..."}` is representable and `identityTrusted` would then silently take the origin branch only.
- **Invariant expression: 6/10** — the doc comment is precise; the struct shape says "any combination".
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — the exclusivity rule and the all-URLs-must-be-listed rule are the security core of the feature and both are correct.
- **Invariant enforcement: 6/10** — `ResolveTrustIdentity` enforces exclusivity and normalization correctly; no other constructor, but nothing stops literals. `DisplayScope()` on the zero value returns `""`, which status/prompt then render as an empty scope.

### Strengths
- `OriginKeyed()` + `DisplayScope()` are the right minimal accessors; callers (`trust_prompt.go:92-97`, `setup.go:1518`, `trust_cmd.go:94`) only use these plus `RemoteName`.
- Path fallback on *any* unparseable URL (rather than partial key set) is the correct fail-closed choice and is tested.

### Concerns
- **Display fields beside the matching key**: `RemoteName`/`Dedicated` are harmless functionally, but they make the type's equality meaningless and blur "what is the consent key". This is a style/clarity issue, not a bug. A cleaner split is `TrustKey` (origins | path) and `TrustIdentity{ Key TrustKey; Remote SyncRemote }`, or just keep `SyncRemote` on `TrustDecision` instead.
- The JSON tags (`origin_keys`, `path`, `remote`, `dedicated`) have no user in the tree — dead surface that implies a serialization contract nobody honors.
- Zero value doubling as "unresolved" means `status --json` can emit `sync_remote: ""` and the prompt can fall back to "this folder only" wording when in fact resolution failed. It is not wrong, but an explicit `Resolved bool`/`error` would make the three states (origin/path/unknown) visible.

### Recommended improvements
1. Make the key a two-case sum: `type TrustKey struct{ origins []string; path string }` with unexported fields and constructors `OriginKey(keys)`/`PathKey(root)`. Cost: moderate (the settings writer `TrustCurrentRepo` iterates `OriginKeys`; expose `Origins() []string`). Benefit: exclusivity becomes unrepresentable-to-violate.
2. Drop the JSON tags until something serializes it. Cost: zero.
3. Cheaper alternative if you keep the flat struct: add `func (id TrustIdentity) valid() bool` and assert it at the end of `ResolveTrustIdentity` (a test-time tripwire). Cost: 3 lines.

---

## Type: `TrustDecision` (repopolicy, `types.go:72`)

### Invariants identified
- `Allowed => Source ∈ {Local, All, Repo} && Reason == None`.
- `!Allowed => Source == None && Reason ∈ {Inactive, Untrusted, InvalidOrigin, Settings}`.
- `Identity` is set whenever it resolved, regardless of `Allowed`; empty under `Inactive`, `InvalidOrigin`, `Settings`.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 3/10** — four exported fields; `Allowed: true, Source: None` is representable.
- **Invariant expression: 5/10** — `Allowed` is redundant with `Source != None`; reason/source are two half-enums of one outcome.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — `Source` drives real UX (banner under `trust_all`, `not_applicable` while tier is off) and `Reason` drives diagnostics.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — `DecideEgress` builds every value correctly and `TrustSourceLocal` is correctly restricted to "tier off".

### Concerns
- **Name collision (style, but a real reading hazard):** `strategy.TrustDecision` (an `int` enum: `TrustHeld`/`TrustGranted`, `trust_prompt.go:18`) and `repopolicy.TrustDecision` (this struct) share a name across two packages that both appear in `manual_commit_push.go`. Rename the strategy one `TrustPromptOutcome` (or `promptResult`). Cost: trivial.
- `computeRepoTrustState` (`status.go:271`) discards `Reason`, so `status --json` cannot distinguish "untrusted" from "user settings file unreadable" (`TrustReasonSettings`) from "election failed" (`TrustReasonInvalidOrigin`). The information exists in the type and is thrown away on the way out. Usefulness gap, cheap to fix (`trust_reason` field).

### Recommended improvements
1. Collapse to `Outcome TrustSource` where `TrustSourceNone` means held, and derive `Allowed()`; keep `Reason` for the held case. Cost: small; removes an impossible state.
2. Surface `Reason` in `globalTrackingJSON`. Cost: 3 lines.

---

## Type: `RepoActivation` (`types.go:121`) and `ReadRepoActivation` (`activation.go:50`)

### Invariants identified
- `Enabled` is meaningful only when `Configured`.
- `LocalOverride => Configured`, and the effective `Enabled` came from a trusted `settings.local.json` with an explicit key.
- A local file without an `enabled` key never sets `Configured`.
- A tracked/symlinked local file is ignored wholesale (via `LocalSettingsTrusted`).

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 4/10** — three bools, any combination constructible; `Enabled: true, Configured: false` is representable and only safe because `policy.go` checks `Configured && Enabled`.
- **Invariant expression: 7/10** — the type comment explains the "set up" notion clearly; `LocalOverride` is well named for its one consumer (the exclusion bypass at `policy.go:99`).
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — `LocalOverride` encodes exactly the trust-relevant fact ("the developer's own action on this clone outranks user exclusions, cloned content does not"); that is the right distinction and it is tested.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — `ReadRepoActivation` is the sole producer and is correct, including the null-`enabled` case.

### Concerns
- Three bools are really a four-state enum: `NotConfigured | ProjectEnabled | ProjectDisabled | Local{enabled bool}`. Modeling it as `type RepoActivation int` (or a small struct with `Source ActivationFile` + `Enabled`) would make `LocalOverride && !Configured` unrepresentable. Style preference; the code is correct as is.
- `LocalOverride` is set to `!isProject` even when no project file exists, so the name "override" is slightly off — it means "came from local", not "overrode project". The doc comment says the right thing; the identifier does not.

### Recommended improvements
- Rename to `FromLocal` or `LocalDecided`. Cost: trivial. Or fold into an enum as above; cost: small, two call sites.

---

## Type: `Repository` (`repository.go:18`)

### Invariants identified
- `WorktreeRoot` and `GitCommonDir` are absolute, symlink-canonicalized.
- `WorktreeKey == runtimeKey(WorktreeID)` (16 hex chars).
- `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` returns `""` when identity incomplete.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 4/10** — `WorktreeKey` is a derived field that can be set independently of `WorktreeID`.
- **Invariant expression: 7/10** — the 64-bit key rationale (collision would merge two worktrees' runtime state) is stated where it matters.
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` being a function of identity alone (not policy) is exactly what uninstall needs and the doc says why.
- **Invariant enforcement: 6/10** — `ResolveRepositoryAt` is the only producer and correct; `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` guards emptiness. But `RuntimeDir(repository)` in `activation.go:19` is a duplicate of `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` **without** the empty guard and has zero callers in the tree — dead code that could be picked up later and reintroduce the empty-root hazard.

### Recommended improvements
1. Delete `RuntimeDir`. Cost: zero.
2. Drop `WorktreeKey` as a field; compute it in `GlobalRuntimeRoot()` from `WorktreeID` (or unexport and expose `Key()`). Cost: small; removes a derivable-field inconsistency.

---

## Types: `SyncRemote`, `SyncRemoteResolver`, and the seams `ResolveSyncRemote` / `LocalSettingsTrusted` (`sync_remote.go`, `activation.go:32`)

### Invariants identified
- `Name == ""` ⇔ no remote ⇒ `URLs` empty ⇒ path identity.
- `URLs` deduplicated; in `Dedicated` mode exactly one derived URL.
- Seams: the real implementations are installed by `settings` (init) and `strategy` (init); the defaults are weaker/different.

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 3/10** — the two seams are exported mutable package globals with no mutex, no `Set…ForTesting` accessor, and no way to tell whether the real implementation is installed.
- **Invariant expression: 7/10** — both defaults document exactly why they exist and what differs; `trust_sync_remote.go` explains the cycle.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — keying consent on the elected remote rather than `origin` is the right invariant, and routing it through one resolver is the right seam.
- **Invariant enforcement: 4/10** — see concerns.

### Concerns (this is the most important design question in the PR)
- **Link-dependent semantics.** `settings` imports `repopolicy` but does not link `strategy`. Every test in `settings` (e.g. `TestTrustCurrentRepoAndRevoke`) therefore runs against the *origin* default, not the election. Any future binary or test package that uses `settings.CheckpointEgressAllowed` without linking `strategy` silently gets pre-election semantics — a consent keyed on `origin` while checkpoints go elsewhere. Today the CLI binary links `strategy`, so production is correct, but the correctness is a property of the link graph, not of the type. Same for `LocalSettingsTrusted`: the repopolicy default (symlink-only) is strictly weaker than the installed one (index + HEAD + symlink), so a repopolicy-only test can pass a case production rejects, or vice versa.
- **Silent unguarded globals.** Tests in both packages reassign the vars and restore in `t.Cleanup`. Correct today only because those specific tests do *not* call `t.Parallel()` while `TestEgressDecision_LocalActivationIsGatedWhileGlobalIsOn` and `TestReadRepoActivation` (which read the seams) do — Go's sequential-then-parallel ordering happens to serialize them. CLAUDE.md says "always use `t.Parallel()`"; the first person who obeys that on one of the seam-mutating tests introduces a `-race` failure. Contrast `paths/invisible.go`, which wraps its test seam in an `RWMutex` — the package is inconsistent with itself.
- `Dedicated` on `SyncRemote` and again on `TrustIdentity` is the same fact copied twice.

### Recommended improvements (ordered by value/cost)
1. **Make "real resolver not installed" loud.** Keep the var but have the default *fail* (`errors.New("repopolicy.ResolveSyncRemote not installed")`) in non-test builds, or record `installed bool` and have `ResolveTrustIdentity` return an error when it is false and `!testing.Testing()`. Cost: ~10 lines. Benefit: converts a silent semantic downgrade into a hard error — this is the one change I would call a real bug-risk reduction.
2. **Replace the bare vars with `Set…ForTesting(fn) (restore func())` accessors guarded by a mutex**, mirroring `paths.SetInvisibleProbeFailureForTesting`. Cost: ~20 lines plus two test call sites. Removes the latent `t.Parallel` race.
3. Longer term: pass a `Resolver` interface through `ClassifyRepoPolicyAt` (a `PolicyDeps{SyncRemote, LocalTrusted}` param with a `Default()` in `settings`). Cost: touches every `ClassifyRepoPolicy` caller (~10). Worth it only if a third seam appears; the accessor approach is the pragmatic stop.

---

## Type: `GlobalConfig` (`types.go:135`)

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 5/10** — plain data, but that is correct for a user-edited file schema. Lists are exported slices mutated in place by `TrustCurrentRepo`/`RevokeCurrentRepo` under `ModifyUserSettings`' lock, which is the right place.
- **Invariant expression: 9/10** — the field docs are the best in the PR: every list states glob-vs-exact, cascade-vs-no-cascade, fail-closed behavior, and why trust fields live in the strict block.
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — the strict-block rationale ("a pre-trust binary must fail closed rather than misread consent") is a genuine safety invariant.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — validation is split correctly: `validateGlobalExclusions` fails closed on activation, `ValidateGlobalPatterns` adds trusted_paths for doctor only. `TrustedOrigins` entries are canonicalized on read (`CanonicalTrustOrigin`) but written raw; fine.

### Concerns
- `TrustAll bool \`json:"trust_all,omitempty"\`` — `omitempty` on a bool means a user who sets `trust_all: false` explicitly will see the key vanish on the next `entire trust` write. Cosmetic, but the file is documented as user-edited, so it is a small surprise.

---

## Type: `UserSettings` (`types.go:209`, `user_settings.go`)

### Invariants identified
- `Global == nil` ⇔ unconfigured tier.
- `global` block strict; other top-level blocks preserved byte-for-byte in `extra`.
- Whole file is one JSON value (trailing-data check).

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 8/10** — `extra` is unexported; the only mutation path is `ModifyUserSettings` (locked, atomic write). Good.
- **Invariant expression: 9/10** — type and method docs state the per-block rule and its reason.
- **Invariant usefulness: 9/10** — forward-compat for mixed-version machines without weakening consent decoding is exactly the right trade.
- **Invariant enforcement: 7/10** — see the receiver issue.

### Concerns
- **Real bug risk (latent):** `MarshalJSON` has a pointer receiver. If any caller ever marshals a `UserSettings` *value* (embeds it by value in another struct, or `json.Marshal(*us)`), `encoding/json` will not find the method, will emit only `global` and **silently drop every preserved block**. Nothing today does that (`persistUserSettings` passes `*UserSettings`), but the failure is silent and destructive to another binary's settings. Make `MarshalJSON` a value receiver (it only reads). Cost: one token.
- `extra` is a map, so copying a `UserSettings` aliases it; harmless because the type is only produced by `LoadUserSettings` and consumed under the lock.
- `"global": null` is skipped on read and not preserved in `extra`, so a round-trip drops the key. Negligible.

---

## Types: `ActivationSource`, `TrustSource`, `TrustReason` (string) vs `InactiveReason` (int)

- **Consistency (style, but it leaks into the API):** three of the four enums are strings with stable wire values and are emitted directly (`string(info.ActivationSource)`); `InactiveReason` is an `int` and needs a hand-written `inactiveReasonJSON` mapper in `status.go:1139` plus `globalInactiveHereText`. Pick one. Strings with stable values are the better fit here since they *are* already a public JSON contract; make `InactiveReason` a string enum with the JSON values it already maps to (`repo_excluded`, `repo_disabled`, `global_off`) and delete the mapper. Cost: small; the `settings` package re-exports the constants so callers do not change.
- **Zero values:** `ActivationSource("")` is not a member (the zero is not `ActivationInactive`), so a zero `RepoPolicy` has an out-of-domain source. `TrustReasonNone == ""` and `InactiveReasonNone == 0` are the zero — inconsistent. Prefer making the zero value the "none/inactive" member for every enum so a zero struct is at least well-formed.
- `InactiveReasonGlobalOff` is overloaded: it is also what `classifyActivationAt` returns when `git rev-parse` fails and what `ClassifyGlobalConfig` returns on a nil resolver. `status.go` sidesteps this via `PolicyError`, but the type itself cannot say "unknown". A `InactiveReasonUnknown`/`ClassificationFailed` member would let the reason stand alone. Cost: one constant + two returns.
- `TrustSourceLocal = "local_activation"` is really "global tier off" (the only way an active repo can hit it). The name reads as "activated locally", which is also true of a repo-enabled repo *with* the tier on — where the source is `repo` or `trust_all`. `TrustSourceTierOff` would be truthful. Style.

---

## Types: `globalTrackingInfo`, `globalTrackingJSON`, `statusJSON` (`status.go`)

### Ratings
- **Encapsulation: 5/10** — unexported struct with exported fields, one producer (`computeGlobalTrackingInfo`); acceptable for an intra-package view model.
- **Invariant expression: 5/10** — five fields carry "meaningless unless X" caveats (`AgentsCovered` unless Enabled; `ActiveHere`/`InactiveReason` unless `InRepo && PolicyError == ""`; `TrustState` "" doubles as the in-repo marker). That is a lot of implicit structure for a flat struct.
- **Invariant usefulness: 8/10** — the "one computation, two renderers" rule is the right invariant and `trackedHere()`/`excludedHere()` capture the two states that matter.
- **Invariant enforcement: 6/10** — the renderers respect the caveats today; nothing stops a new renderer from reading `ActiveHere` when `PolicyError != ""`.

### Concerns
- The comment at `status.go:1183` — "TrustState doubles as the in-repo marker" — is a smell: `InRepo` already exists. Use it.
- `PolicyError` and `ActiveHere` are mutually exclusive by convention only. A small nested `*repoView{ Active, InactiveReason, TrustState, TrustSource, SyncRemote, Held }` set only on successful classification would make the "outside a repo" and "classification failed" shapes structurally different from "classified". Cost: moderate refactor of one file; only worth it if more fields are coming (they probably are).
- As noted under `TrustDecision`: `trust_reason` is dropped from JSON.

---

## Types: `strategy.TrustDecision` / `trustChoice` (`trust_prompt.go`)

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 8, Expression 8, Usefulness 8, Enforcement 8.** Small, unexported choice enum; the outcome enum is two-valued and the comment on `TrustGranted` ("the caller re-evaluates the gate, never reuses this as a boolean") is exactly the right invariant, and `manual_commit_push.go:84-111` honors it by reclassifying. `askTrustPrompt` starting with `trustChoice("")` and whitelisting the three values before returning is good accessible-mode hygiene.
- Only concern is the cross-package name clash already noted. Rename to `trustPromptOutcome`/`TrustPromptOutcome`.

---

## Type: `CheckpointSyncRemote` / `CheckpointSyncRemoteSource` (`checkpoint_sync_remote.go`)

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 5, Expression 8, Usefulness 8, Enforcement 6.** The precedence doc is thorough and the source enum matches `status --json`.
- **Real (minor) bug risk:** `ResolveCheckpointSyncRemoteForTrust` (`trust_sync_remote.go:60`) fabricates `Source: SyncRemoteSourceConfig` for an `--remote` override. The type now lies about provenance; if any renderer or `hintGatedCheckpointSync`-style check (`Source == SyncRemoteSourceConfig` suppresses the hint) ever consumes this value, it will treat a one-off override as a persistent setting. Add `SyncRemoteSourceOverride` (or return only the name). Cost: one constant.

---

## `paths/invisible.go` — `ErrUnroutableRuntimePath`, test seam

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 8, Expression 8, Usefulness 9, Enforcement 7.** Sentinel + `Is` helper, fail-closed on mismatch, and the worktree-identity check before trusting a ctx snapshot is a good defensive invariant. The mutex-guarded test seam is the pattern `repopolicy` should copy.
- Gap: does not reject `policy.RuntimeRoot() == ""` (see `RepoPolicy`). One `if root == "" { return "", ErrUnroutableRuntimePath }` closes it at the choke point regardless of what `repopolicy` does.

---

## `internal/worktreeid`

- **Ratings: Encapsulation 8, Expression 7, Usefulness 8, Enforcement 7.** Pure functions, clear main-vs-linked contract, submodule-aware parsing. Two independent hashes of the same ID exist (`worktreeid.Hash` = 6 chars for branch names, `repopolicy.runtimeKey` = 16 for directories); the reason is documented at `runtimeKey`. Fine, but consider `worktreeid.HashN(id, n)` so the two derivations share one function. Cost: trivial.

---

## Summary: real bug risks vs. style

**Real bug risks (fix in this PR or a fast follow):**
1. `UserSettings.MarshalJSON` pointer receiver — a value marshal silently drops preserved blocks. One-token fix.

## Findings

### Critical

**1. `entire enable` in an excluded repo silently records machine-wide egress consent**
`cmd/entire/cli/setup.go:1501` (`recordEnableTrust`, called at `:1386`, `:1474`, `:2045`)

`recordEnableTrust` gates only on `us.GlobalEnabled()`. In a repo the classifier carves out (`InactiveReasonGlobalExcluded`) — or one it fails to classify — `settings.CheckpointEgressAllowed(ctx)` returns false because `policy.Active` is false, so the guard falls through and `settings.TrustCurrentRepo(ctx)` writes the repo's origin key into `global.trusted_origins`. `TrustCurrentRepo` resolves the identity independently of activation, so the write succeeds. Then the post-write re-check still fails and the user gets:

> `Warning: trust for github.com/acme/widgets was written to <path>, but checkpoint sync is still held — check that file's trust entries.`

Two problems: the message misdiagnoses the cause (exclusion, not a bad trust entry), and `trusted_origins` is a **machine-wide, origin-keyed** grant — every *other*, non-excluded clone of `github.com/acme/widgets` on this machine now syncs without ever being asked. This is exactly what `trust_cmd.go:111` `refuseTrustWhenInactive` exists to prevent ("silently pre-consenting an excluded repo is the bug consent exists to prevent"); `enable` bypasses that guard. This path is exercised today by `TestStatus_ExcludedRepoWithRepoSetup`, which calls `runEnable(..., true)` and only asserts on the exclusion note.

Fix: make `recordEnableTrust` share `trust`'s precondition — return before writing unless the repo is actually active:

```go
if active, _ := settings.IsActiveForRepoWithReason(ctx); !active {
    return // noteExcludedAfterEnable explains why
}
```

and swap the call order so `noteExcludedAfterEnable` runs first (today the "Note: … keeps it inactive here" line also prints *before* "Entire is now enabled.", which reads backwards).

---

### Important

**2. Three unmemoized repository classifications per hook process**
`cmd/entire/cli/config.go:120` (`newLogger`), with `root.go:106` and `hook_registry.go:109`

`newLogger` now calls `paths.AbsPath(ctx, logging.LogsDir)`, which routes into `paths.runtimeRootForPath` → `repopolicy.ClassifyRepoPolicy(ctx)` whenever no snapshot is on `ctx`. The root `PersistentPreRun` calls `settings.IsActiveForRepo` (classification #1, replacing main's cheap `IsSetUpAny` stat), then `ensureLogger` → `newLogger` (#2), then `prepareHookPolicy` (#3) — and `ensureLogger` attaches only the *logger* to the context, never the policy, so nothing downstream can reuse it.

`ClassifyRepoPolicy` is not memoized: each call spawns `git rev-parse --show-toplevel --git-common-dir`, resolves the worktree ID, reads the user settings file, and (when `exclude_origins` is set) reads the origin fetch+push URLs. `paths.WorktreeRoot` is memoized precisely because this path is hot; CLAUDE.md documents the same class of regression for the OPF trust probe (8.3ms → 2.5ms per hook process, 39ms → 11ms on reftable). This lands on every agent hook and every git hook.

Fix: classify once in the root `PersistentPreRun` and attach it — `cmd.SetContext(repopolicy.WithRepoPolicy(ctx, policy))` — before `ensureLogger`. Both `prepareHookPolicy` and `runtimeRootForPath` already short-circuit on a context snapshot, so this collapses 3 classifications to 1. Alternatively memoize `ResolveRepositoryAt`/`ClassifyRepoPolicy` per cwd inside `repopolicy`.

**3. `entire trust` reports "global tracking is off" when it is verifiably on**
`cmd/entire/cli/trust_cmd.go:136`

`refuseTrustWhenInactive` reaches this line only after `us.GlobalEnabled()` returned true, so the message is always false there. It is reached in two real cases:
- `InactiveReasonRepoDisabled` — the repo's own `.entire/settings*.json` carries `enabled: false`. The user is told to enable global tracking (already on) instead of to fix the repo veto.
- Classification error — `IsActiveForRepoWithReason` returns `(false, InactiveReasonNone)` on any error, so an unclassifiable repo also gets the wrong explanation.

Fix: branch on the reason rather than falling through to one message:

```go
switch reason {
case settings.InactiveReasonGlobalExcluded: // existing text
case settings.InactiveReasonRepoDisabled:
    // "Entire is disabled in this repository's settings; run 'entire enable' first."
default:
    // "This repository could not be classified; run 'entire doctor'."
}
```

**4. `disable --uninstall` leaves the machine-wide trust grant behind, and its note doesn't say so**
`cmd/entire/cli/setup.go:2597`

The closing note says the next session "will track this repo again unless you add it to `exclude_paths`". But the `trusted_origins`/`trusted_paths` entry written by the earlier `entire enable` (finding 1) or by `entire trust` is *not* removed by uninstall, so the repo will be re-captured **and re-synced** with no prompt — the user reasonably reads "uninstalled" as "nothing leaves this machine any more". Note also that the sentence has no early exit for a repo with recorded trust.

Fix: when trust is recorded for this repo, extend the note (`…will track this repo again, and its checkpoints will sync — trust for <scope> is still recorded in <path>; run 'entire trust --revoke' to withdraw it`), or call `settings.RevokeCurrentRepo` as part of the uninstall steps.

---

### Suggestions

**5. `heldCheckpointCount` omits the dedicated-remote guard that `computeCheckpointSyncInfo` documents**
